plan.question: How did routine maintenance destroy the world's most productive oil platform?

chapters.title: The Steel Fortress
beats: In the deep waters off Scotland, a thirty-four-thousand-tonne steel oil platform dominated ten percent of North Sea production.
A sudden gas leak and an uncontrollable fire brought the entire structure crashing down, claiming one hundred and sixty-seven lives.
The catastrophe revealed how easily a modern industrial marvel could collapse when routine maintenance went unnoticed across shifts.

chapters.title: Ten Percent of the Sea
beats: Occidental Petroleum secured an exploration licence and discovered the massive Piper oilfield deep in the North Sea.
The company commissioned a giant eight-legged steel jacket to pump oil, starting commercial flow at two hundred and fifty thousand barrels per day.
Major works were added in 1978 to extract and transport gas under intense pressure to satisfy government conservation requirements.
William Cullen would later be tasked with examining how this complex maze of high-pressure lines and shift handovers was managed.
chapters.hook: A routine summer revamp was about to test that network to its limit.

chapters.title: The Unsigned Paperwork
beats: By July 1988, major construction, maintenance, and upgrade works were planned, leaving the platform undergoing a complex revamp.
At 07:45 on 6 July 1988, permit-to-work forms for the incoming day shift were issued and signed for routine equipment servicing.
Work began on critical condensate equipment, setting up a situation where safety-critical hardware was removed while the platform continued operating.
Heat from burning oil caused the Tartan pipeline to rupture violently.
The fracture instantly discharged thirty tonnes of highly flammable gas in the first minute alone.
The massive gas release ignited into a sustained, unquenchable jet fire directly beneath the platform decks.
chapters.hook: The steel fortress was now sitting above an open furnace.

chapters.title: Collapse into the Sea
beats: Through the night between 6 and 7 July 1988, continuous high-pressure gas jet fires battered the platform structure without stopping.
Piper Alpha suffered catastrophic explosions and structural collapse into the sea, killing one hundred and sixty-seven people and leaving only sixty-one survivors.
Thirty bodies were never recovered from the deep water, and insured losses eventually climbed to 1.7 billion pounds.
On 28 March 1989, salvage crews toppled the burned and unstable remains of the platform into the sea.

chapters.title: The Cullen Report
beats: In November 1990, William Cullen issued the official inquiry report, concluding that an initial condensate leak was caused by maintenance work.
Cullen's findings led the British government to overhaul North Sea industry standards by enacting the Offshore Safety Act 1992.
The Offshore Installations (Safety Case) Regulations 1992 were enacted, forcing operators to formally prove their safety controls before drilling.
